Playwright browser contexts provide isolated cookies, cache, and storage; request interception can cover context-wide traffic, and service workers should be blocked because otherwise they can hide requests from interception. [Playwright isolation](https://playwright.dev/docs/browser-contexts), [Playwright networking](https://playwright.dev/docs/network)
- Feed the already-staged main HTML response to Chromium at its final URL, then send every subresource request through the same safe fetch gateway.
- Use a deterministic viewport, locale, color scheme, and user agent, and record these in the capture manifest.
- Wait for `DOMContentLoaded`, then a short quiet period, with an absolute deadline. Optionally perform bounded scrolling to trigger common lazy-loaded images; never click, submit, authenticate, grant permissions, or dismiss consent prompts automatically.
- Treat Chromium’s `Page.captureSnapshot`/MHTML capability as a transient capture aid, not as the served artifact. It can preserve frame and shadow-DOM material, but the result remains active content and is Chromium-specific. [Chrome DevTools Protocol Page domain](https://chromedevtools.github.io/devtools-protocol/tot/Page/)
- Produce a static bundle:
  - Sanitized main document.
  - Sanitized CSS.
  - Content-addressed local assets.
  - Manifest containing original URL, effective URL, capture time, hashes, byte sizes, media types, missing-resource warnings, and capture/sanitizer versions.
- Rewrite every retained resource reference to an internal immutable asset identifier. Remove `<base>`, service-worker registrations, manifests, preloads/prefetches, remote CSS imports, refresh directives, and any URL that was not captured.
- Remove scripts, inline event handlers, forms and form controls, frames, objects/embeds, media autoplay, custom protocol links, downloads, and active SVG content. Replace frames/video/audio with a static placeholder or poster and a warning; they are explicitly outside faithful static reproduction.
- Parse CSS with a real CSS parser and reserialize it. Do not use regex. Rewrite known asset URLs and remove `@import`, remote URLs, and unsupported active constructs.
- Decode and re-encode images, especially SVG, rather than serving arbitrary image bytes directly. Omit remote fonts in v1 and use system fallbacks; this slightly reduces visual fidelity but removes a substantial parser and tracking surface.
- Store an optional full-page screenshot as a diagnostic/fidelity aid, not as the readable copy.

### PDF preservation

- Store the exact successfully delivered body bytes; do not reserialize, optimize, or convert them.
- Compute SHA-256 while downloading and persist the digest and size in the manifest.
- Require:
  - a successful final HTTP response,
  - no truncation or limit breach,
  - consistency with `Content-Length` when present,
  - PDF header recognition,
  - successful structural parsing,
  - successful rendering of at least the first page.
- Keep the original PDF blob immutable.
- View it through a pinned PDF.js-based viewer in a separate sandboxed origin with external navigation, JavaScript actions, attachments, form submission, and network access disabled. Offer an explicit “download retained original” action separately. This preserves the original file while avoiding direct trust in PDF actions or browser plug-in behavior.
- Password-protected, malformed, or oversized PDFs should end as `failed` with a specific explanation. A future password-entry flow can be added without weakening the initial design.

## SSRF and worker isolation

URL validation alone is insufficient. Use layered controls:

- Put all capture browser traffic through an egress proxy/gateway; deny direct network access from capture workers.
- Resolve and inspect all A and AAAA answers. Reject loopback, private, link-local, unique-local, multicast, unspecified, documentation/test, reserved, and cloud metadata destinations.
- Resolve and validate again at connection time, then pin the selected public address for that request. Revalidate every redirect and every subresource. OWASP calls out DNS pinning/rebinding and recommends checking all A/AAAA results. [OWASP SSRF guidance](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Server_Side_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html)
- Reject URL user-info, ambiguous numeric IP forms, invalid IDNs, fragments for fetching, and non-HTTP schemes.
- Permit ports 80 and 443 by default. Supporting arbitrary public ports should be an explicit later decision because it greatly expands scan capability.
- Block WebSocket/WebRTC/QUIC and non-proxied DNS.
- Run the renderer as an unprivileged process/container with:
  - no app/database/cloud credentials,
  - read-only root filesystem,
  - isolated temporary directory,
  - PID, memory, CPU, file-descriptor, and process-count limits,
  - no host mounts,
  - Chromium sandbox retained,
  - a current pinned browser build.
- Do not pass the user’s browser cookies or authenticated app session into capture.

Relevant reserved ranges include IPv4 private space and link-local space; coverage must also include the corresponding IPv6 categories. [RFC 1918](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1918.html), [RFC 3927](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3927.html), [RFC 4193](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4193.html)

## Safe offline viewing

Serve saved pages only through a dedicated snapshot origin, not the application origin, and embed them in an iframe with an empty `sandbox` attribute—no `allow-scripts`, `allow-same-origin`, `allow-forms`, `allow-popups`, navigation, or download tokens. The HTML standard says this combination forces an opaque origin and blocks scripts, forms, downloads, popups, and navigation; it also warns that hostile files should not be served from the application server. [WHATWG iframe sandbox](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/iframe-embed-object.html), [WHATWG sandbox flags](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/browsers.html)

Apply response headers as defense in depth:

```text
Content-Security-Policy:
  default-src 'none';
  img-src 'self' data:;
  style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline';
  font-src 'self';
  script-src 'none';
  connect-src 'none';
  frame-src 'none';
  object-src 'none';
  media-src 'none';
  worker-src 'none';
  form-action 'none';
  base-uri 'none';
  sandbox
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
Referrer-Policy: no-referrer
Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-site
Cache-Control: private, immutable
```

CSP defines `default-src`, `script-src`, `connect-src`, `object-src`, `base-uri`, `form-action`, and `sandbox` for these controls. [CSP Level 3](https://www.w3.org/TR/CSP/)

Also:

- Never interpolate snapshot markup into the app DOM.
- Serve assets using manifest-authorized opaque IDs, not arbitrary file paths or proxied URLs.
- Disable content disposition tricks and supply known media types with `nosniff`.
- Render links visually but route activation through an explicit app-controlled “Open original link” confirmation/action. The snapshot itself should not navigate.
- Ensure viewing succeeds with all outbound network disabled.

## Limits

Recommended configurable v1 defaults:

| Limit | Default |
|---|---:|
| Redirect hops | 5 |
| DNS/connect timeout per request | 5 s |
| Main response header timeout | 10 s |
| Total HTML capture wall time | 45 s |
| Post-DOM quiet wait | 5 s |
| Total requests | 500 |
| Single asset | 15 MiB |
| Total stored HTML bundle | 100 MiB |
| PDF size | 250 MiB |
| Nested frame depth | 3 |
| Automatic transient retries | 3 with exponential backoff |

A limit breach must produce a stable error code such as `too_large`, `too_many_resources`, `timeout`, `blocked_destination`, `unsupported_type`, or `render_failed`. Do not label a truncated capture “available.” Missing nonessential resources may produce an available capture with warnings only if validation proves that retained primary text and essential images remain readable.

## Immutable replacement semantics

Model attempts and completed artifacts separately:

- `CaptureAttempt`: queued/running/available/failed/cancelled, bookmark ID, URL revision, source URL, timing, error code/detail, retry count, progress.
- `SavedCopy`: immutable ID, kind, source/effective URL, captured timestamp, manifest key/hash, total size, capture and sanitizer versions.
- `SavedCopyAsset`: copy ID, logical path, content digest, media type, size.
- Bookmark stores a pointer to its current available saved copy.

Rules:

- Saving the bookmark and inserting the initial queued attempt happen in one transaction.
- A worker builds into temporary storage. Only after full validation does one database transaction publish the `SavedCopy` and change the attempt to `available`.
- Retry creates a new attempt; it never mutates an available copy.
- Explicit recapture builds a candidate copy first. It replaces the bookmark pointer only after success and explicit user confirmation.
- If the bookmark URL changes during capture, the completed copy retains the old source URL and is shown as belonging to the earlier address. It must not be relabeled.
- A failed replacement leaves the previous available copy untouched.
- Permanent deletion first makes the bookmark and copy inaccessible transactionally, then performs idempotent blob cleanup. Content-addressed assets are physically removed only when no saved copy references them.

This design satisfies the “never silently replaced” requirement while avoiding a failure window where a good copy is lost.

## Background processing

Use a durable database-backed job queue/outbox for the initial implementation:

- Bookmark creation transaction inserts the bookmark, `pending` capture attempt, and outbox record. This makes status visible immediately and prevents lost jobs.
- Workers lease jobs with a heartbeat; expired leases are reclaimable.
- Use an idempotency key based on attempt ID. Reprocessing the same job must converge on the same result.
- Retry only transient failures automatically; validation, unsupported type, policy rejection, and size-limit failures require user action.
- Bound renderer concurrency independently from fetch concurrency; recommended initial renderer concurrency is 2 per host.
- Imports enqueue attempts in batches and expose queued/running/succeeded/failed totals without waiting for capture completion.
- Deleting a bookmark cancels queued/running attempts and makes any late worker commit fail its URL-revision/deletion check.

## Validation strategy

Before publishing an HTML copy:

- Verify manifest and asset hashes/sizes.
- Parse HTML and assert there are no scripts, event attributes, forms, frames, embeds/objects, refresh directives, active SVG, `srcdoc`, remote URLs, or unrecognized URL-bearing attributes.
- Parse CSS and assert there are no imports or nonlocal URLs.
- Confirm every retained reference resolves to a manifest asset.
- Open the snapshot in Playwright with networking forced offline and fail all requests; assert zero attempted external requests.
- Assert primary visible text remains. A useful automated quality gate is at least 95% retention of normalized visible text measured before sanitization, except content explicitly classified as unsupported.
- Exercise an adversarial corpus covering script/event execution, meta refresh, form submission, downloads, popups, iframe navigation, CSS imports, SVG scripts, service workers, WebSockets, malformed markup, redirect loops, rebinding, and all blocked IP classes.
- Add golden-page tests for layout, images, Unicode, responsive CSS, lazy loading, and missing assets.
- For PDFs, compare stored SHA-256 to the streaming ingest hash, parse the stored bytes again, render a page offline, and verify no network calls.
- Run acceptance tests with the original server disabled, not merely with a copied URL still reachable.

## Alternatives considered

- **Raw MHTML as the user-facing copy:** highest apparent fidelity and simple packaging, but retains active content, is browser-specific, and is difficult to sanitize safely. Use only as a transient capture source or debugging artifact.
- **Reader-mode extraction only:** easiest and safest, but fails the approved requirement to retain recognizable structure, styling, and essential images.
- **Full-page screenshot:** visually faithful but not a readable/searchable structured copy and inaccessible to assistive technology.
- **WARC/WACZ preservation:** strong archival provenance, but requires a replay stack and replay isolation; it is better as a future export/archive format than the initial reading format.
- **Serving sanitized snapshots from the app origin:** simpler deployment, but the blast radius of sanitizer or browser defects is too high. A separate snapshot origin and sandbox are worth the operational cost.
- **Direct browser PDF embedding:** simpler, but gives less control over embedded PDF actions, external links, and viewer behavior than an isolated PDF.js viewer.

## Main residual risks

- No generic crawler can faithfully preserve authenticated, heavily interactive, canvas/WebGL, DRM, paywalled, or continuously updating applications.
- Consent overlays and lazy content can hide the article without prohibited interaction; the UI should surface capture warnings and retry.
- Sanitizing CSS/images inevitably creates some fidelity loss.
- Browser and PDF/image parsers remain attack surfaces, so worker isolation, patching, and resource limits are mandatory.
- Deduplicated content-addressed storage can leak equality information if ever made multi-user; scope hashes and authorization carefully if accounts are added.
- A “95% representative pages” success criterion needs a versioned representative corpus and an agreed definition of “essential image”; otherwise the metric is not reproducible.
